subject: numeric overflow in Von Mises distribution

messages.author: 6487b51683782747
messages.subject: numeric overflow in Von Mises distribution
parts:
Hi.  I’m trying to build a model with the Von Mises distribution in rstan, but so far it’s been crashed in <10 samples by a numeric overflow generated by boost::math::cyl_bessel_i<d>(d,d) (demo and session info attached).  I’m using a domain (-pi, pi) in the code, but the problem occurs with (0, 2pi) as well, and with a more restricted prior on kappa.

 

From the list, it looks like the von_mises implementation is new in stan 2.0.x, so I’m guessing it hasn’t been used much and this is just due to a missing exception handler.  Could there be a different problem?

 

Thanks,

 

Nate

 

--

Nathanael Lichti

Postdoctoral Research Assistant

Forestry and Natural Resources

Purdue University

715 W. State St.

West Lafayette, IN 47907

nli...@purdue.edu

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] numeric overflow in Von Mises distribution
parts:
You're right --- I don't think it's gotten a lot of play (or obviously
enough testing).

Do you know what values of y, mu and kappa are causing the problem?
You could replace

y ~ von_mises(mu, kappa);

with

print("mu=",mu);
print("kappa=",kappa);
for (n in 1:N) {
print("n=",n, "; y=",y);
y[n] ~ von_mises(mu, kappa);
}

We should at least be catching that exception and just rejecting
the sample as of the next release (2.2.0). We weren't previously catching
all the errors thrown by Boost functions.

We were hoping to get 2.2.0 out this week, but our continuous integration
server is being flaky and we're all swamped with side projects. (Excuses,
excuses, I know.)

- Bob

messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] numeric overflow in Von Mises distribution
parts:
I appreciate the enthusiasm, Andrew. Thanks!

Bob, I inserted the print statements and ran some more tests. It looks like the issue is with large values for kappa. I tried inserted

print("besselI = ", modified_bessel_first_kind(0, kappa));

in the model statement before the sampling loop that you suggested, and that also caused the error. So I changed the model to

data{
int<lower = 0> N;
real<lower = 0> kappa;
}
parameters{
real mu;
}
model{
for (n in 1:N) {

print("n=",n, "; y=", kappa[n]);
print("besselI = ", modified_bessel_first_kind(0, kappa[n]));
increment_log_prob(normal_log(kappa[n],mu , 1));
}

And used data,

vm_dat = list(N = 14, kappa = c(0, exp(0:12)))

This produced the error at n = 9, kappa = 1096.63. The preceding value (kappa = 403.429) gave Bessel I = 3.19e+173.

Do the boost functions have the option to work on an exponential scale? If so, that could solve the issue. For example, see the BesselI function in the R package Bessel.

messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] numeric overflow in Von Mises distribution
parts:
Sorry - that should have been defined as kappa[N]. Typo in the email.

A kappa of 400 corresponds to a standard deviation of about 3 degrees or 0.05 radians. So depending on the application, much higher values might be reasonable. In my case, I'm modeling error in directional measurements for mapping data, and it's plausible that in some cases most errors may be as small as 0.1 degree, which would give a kappa > 1e7. Happily, I'm also working with short distances, so there's not any practical difference between a 3 degree error and an 0.1 degree error once I translate back to an (x,y) plane. If I need to, I can just put an upper limit on kappa to prevent the overflow, but it would be nice to have an unbiased estimate of precision.

I'll try updating boost and see if that works, and if not, I'm going to try rescaling the measurements with a redundant parameterization. Will let you know how it goes in a few days. Thanks for the help.

messages.author: 6487b51683782747
messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] numeric overflow in Von Mises distribution
parts:
Hi. I haven't tested boost 1.55 yet, but I found a couple of workarounds that do the job with 1.54. The first was to rescale the data to an interval of 2*pi, fit the von Mises, and estimate kappa from a back-transformed posterior predictive sample (code below). However, because Stan includes conditional processing (I love this!), a cleaner solution uses the fact that asymptotically, as kappa -> Inf, VM(mu, kappa) -> N(mu, sqrt(1/kappa)). So this code yields very good results as long as kappa_star is reasonable:

data{
... define N, y ...
real<lower = 0> kappa_star; // e.g., 100; use normal approx. for kappa >= kappa_star
}
...
model{
for(n in 1:N){
if(kappa < kappa_star)
increment_log_prob(von_mises_log(y[n], mu, kappa));
else
increment_log_prob(normal_log(y[n], mu, sqrt(1/kappa))); // normal approximation
}
}

By the way, I tried using vectorized sampling statements in place of the manual increment, and with kappa = 2e6, Stan slowed to the point that I thought it had hung. I only tried it once, so it could have just been a coincidence. With kappa = 2, the vectorized version was about 5 seconds faster over 1000 draws.

- Nate

Here's code for the first approach:

data{
...
int<lower = 0> M; // number of posterior predictive samples generate
}
...
transformed data{
real<lower = 0, upper = 2 * pi()> z[N];
real<lower = 1> scale_factor;

scale_factor <- 2 * pi() / (max(y) - min(y));
for(n in 1:N)
z[n] <- (y[n] - min(y)) * scale_factor;
}
... define mu_z and kappa_z parameters ...
model{
z ~ von_mises(mu_z, kappa_z);
}
generated quantities{ // assuming syntax is right - I did this in R
real<lower = 0, upper = 2 * pi()> z_star[M]; // posterior predicted z
real<lower = 0, upper = 2 * pi()> y_star[M]; // back-transformation z -> y
real<lower = 0, upper = 2 * pi()> mu; // mean of y
real<lower = 0> var_y_star; // variance of y_star
real<lower = 0> kappa_approx; // approximate concentration of y

mu <- mu_z / scale_factor + min(y);
for(m in 1:M){
z_star[m] ~ von_mises(mu_z, kappa_z);
y_star[m] <- z_star[m] / scale_factor + min(y);
}
var_y_star <- sum(pow(y_star - mu, 2)) / (M - 1);
kappa_approx <- 1/var_y_star; // kappa_approx -> kappa as kappa -> Inf

}
